blocks.text: Ridge Regression demonstrated regularization concretely, shrinking every coefficient while keeping every feature in the model. Lasso regression takes the L1 penalty first introduced back in the Feature Selection module and gives it the genuine full treatment here, as a complete regression algorithm in its own right, one that genuinely performs feature selection automatically as a direct, natural consequence of fitting itself.

This topic covers the L1 penalty Lasso adds, recapped here as the primary technique rather than a brief comparison point, a genuinely deeper, geometric explanation for why L1 produces exactly zero coefficients while L2 does not, why Lasso genuinely requires iterative optimization rather than a direct, closed form solution, when to genuinely prefer Lasso over Ridge for a specific, real problem, and LassoCV, the standard tool for automating the alpha selection this technique depends on.
1. The L1 Penalty, Now as the Primary Technique

blocks.alt: Linear regression with an added L1 penalty becomes lasso regression

blocks.text: Lasso regression genuinely adds alpha, a chosen strength parameter, multiplied by the genuine sum of the absolute values of every feature coefficient, directly to the standard mean squared error loss. This is genuinely the exact same L1 penalty first covered back in the Feature Selection module Lasso topic, here it becomes the actual, central subject rather than a technique introduced specifically for its feature selection side effect.

The genuine mechanics are identical to what was covered there, larger coefficients cost more under this penalty, and the model genuinely balances fitting the data well against keeping that total penalty cost low.
2. A Genuinely Deeper, Geometric Explanation

blocks.alt: The L1 constraint forms a diamond shape whose sharp corners hit zero

blocks.text: Picturing the L2 penalty Ridge uses as a genuine constraint region produces a smooth circle, with no sharp corners, meaning the optimal solution rarely lands precisely on an axis, where a coefficient would genuinely equal zero. The L1 penalty Lasso uses, by genuine contrast, produces a constraint region shaped like a diamond, with real, sharp corners that sit exactly on the axes.

Because the mathematically optimal solution genuinely tends to land at a corner of this diamond shaped region, and those corners are exactly where one or more coefficients genuinely equal zero, Lasso solutions are genuinely, structurally more likely to have some coefficients land at precisely zero. This is genuinely the deeper, geometric reason behind the exact zero property first stated back in the Feature Selection Lasso topic, now actually explained rather than simply asserted.

blocks.text: 3. Why Lasso Genuinely Needs Iterative Optimization

blocks.alt: Lasso loss is not smooth everywhere, so it needs an iterative solver

blocks.text: The L1 penalty absolute value function has a genuine sharp corner at exactly zero, mathematically, it is genuinely not differentiable there, which means the direct, closed form solution available to Ridge, covered in the previous topic, simply does not exist for Lasso. Instead, Lasso is genuinely solved through an iterative technique called coordinate descent, repeatedly optimizing one coefficient at a time while holding the others fixed, cycling through every coefficient until the solution genuinely converges.

This is a genuinely real, practical distinction worth remembering directly, not just a mathematical footnote, it explains why Ridge fits essentially instantly while Lasso fitting can genuinely take measurably longer, especially on datasets with many features.
4. A Worked Example

blocks.alt: Ten features fit with lasso leave 4 surviving features

blocks.text: Fitting Lasso directly on a dataset with one genuinely irrelevant feature shows the automatic selection in action, extending the exact same worked example first used back in the Feature Selection Lasso topic.

code.content:
from sklearn.linear_model import Lasso
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import pandas as pd

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "square_feet": [900, 1200, 1500, 1800, 2100, 2400],
    "bedrooms": [2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5],
    "shoe_size_unrelated": [8, 9, 7, 10, 8, 9],
})
y = pd.Series([250000, 310000, 360000, 410000, 460000, 510000])

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
model = Lasso(alpha=5000)
model.fit(X_scaled, y)

print(dict(zip(X.columns, model.coef_)))

blocks.text: With a genuinely strong enough alpha, shoe_size_unrelated coefficient genuinely lands at exactly 0.0, the model automatically, structurally excluding it as a direct, natural consequence of the fitting process itself, exactly the geometric corner solution covered above.

blocks.text: 5. When to Genuinely Prefer Lasso Over Ridge

blocks.alt: Suspecting many useless features points toward preferring lasso

blocks.text: Lasso genuinely makes more sense when there is real reason to believe many available features are actually irrelevant, and automatic, built in feature selection is genuinely desired as part of the model itself. Ridge genuinely makes more sense when most features are believed to carry at least some real signal, and the goal is genuinely stabilizing and dampening every coefficient rather than eliminating any of them entirely.

This is genuinely a real, practical decision worth making deliberately for a specific dataset, rather than defaulting to one or the other automatically, the right choice depends directly on a genuine belief about how sparse the real, underlying relationship actually is.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Choosing between Ridge and Lasso genuinely comes down to a real belief about sparsity, whether many features are genuinely irrelevant, Lasso, or most carry at least some real signal, Ridge.

blocks.text: 6. LassoCV: Automating the Alpha Search

blocks.alt: Many alpha values are tried and cross validated to find the best one

blocks.text: Rather than manually trying several genuine alpha values by hand and comparing results, LassoCV genuinely automates that entire search using cross validation, a technique covered in full depth in its own dedicated module later in this course, returning the alpha value that genuinely performed best empirically across multiple validation splits.

This is genuinely the standard, practical way alpha actually gets chosen in a real project, removing the guesswork from manually picking a single, specific alpha value and replacing it with a genuine, systematic, data driven search.

blocks.title: A practical habit
blocks.content: Reach for LassoCV by default over manually specifying a single alpha value, unless there is a genuine, specific reason to fix it directly, such as matching a previously deployed model exactly.

blocks.text: 7. The Result: A Genuinely Sparse Final Model

Given genuinely many input features, some carrying real signal and some genuinely irrelevant, Lasso fitting process automatically zeros out the irrelevant ones, producing a genuinely sparse final model, one that retains only the features that actually earned their place, with zero manual feature selection work required beyond choosing alpha.

This is genuinely the complete, real payoff of this entire technique, feature selection and model fitting happen together, in one single, genuine training pass, rather than as two genuinely separate steps the way the filter and wrapper methods covered back in Feature Selection required.
8. Lasso Regression Versus What Comes Next

blocks.alt: Lasso regression is covered here, elastic net comes next

blocks.text: Ridge and Lasso together cover the genuine two ends of the regularization spectrum, keep everything but shrink, versus automatically select a sparse subset. A genuinely natural question follows directly, why not get some of both benefits at once.

The next topic, Elastic Net, does exactly that, genuinely combining the L1 and L2 penalties together into a single technique, blending Ridge stability under correlated features with Lasso automatic feature selection.

items: Lasso regression genuinely gives the L1 penalty its full treatment as a complete regression algorithm.
Its diamond shaped constraint region genuinely explains, geometrically, why coefficients can land exactly at zero.
Lasso genuinely requires iterative coordinate descent, since the L1 penalty is not differentiable at exactly zero.
Prefer Lasso when many features are genuinely believed irrelevant; prefer Ridge when most carry real signal.
LassoCV genuinely automates the alpha search using cross validation, rather than manual trial and error.
The next topic, Elastic Net, genuinely combines L1 and L2 together into a single, blended technique.
